evidence.quote: Mr Birdsey had been doing something which he had not done since he left New York five years ago. He had been watching a game of baseball.
evidence.paraphrase: The protagonist has been geographically separated from his home city for five years.

evidence.quote: He loved baseball with a love passing the love of women, and the prospect of never seeing a game again in his life appalled him.
evidence.paraphrase: Birdsey is dismayed at the prospect of never seeing baseball again.

evidence.quote: The man gave a start that was almost a leap, and the pallor of his face became a sickly white. His eyes, as he swung round, met Mr Birdsey's for an instant before they dropped, and there was panic fear in them.
evidence.paraphrase: The bearded man reacts with sudden panic and fear when tapped on the shoulder.

evidence.quote: If I think I remember a face, and can't place it, I worry myself into insomnia. It's partly sheer vanity, and partly because in my job a good memory for faces is a mighty fine asset.
evidence.paraphrase: Waterall describes his method of identifying faces from memory as central to his work.

evidence.quote: This is Mr John Benyon, and I last saw him five years ago when I was a reporter in New York, and covered his trial.
evidence.paraphrase: The bearded stranger is revealed to be a fugitive whose identity Waterall recalls from a past trial.

evidence.quote: He robbed the New Asiatic Bank of a hundred thousand dollars, jumped his bail, and was never heard of again.
evidence.paraphrase: Benyon's past crime and flight explain his years of hidden exile.

evidence.quote: It was because I was a dead man, and saw a chance of coming to life for a day; because I was sick of the damned tomb I've been living in for five centuries; because I've been aching for New York ever since I've left it
evidence.paraphrase: Benyon explains he risked capture out of longing for home after years of miserable exile.

evidence.quote: The next moment Benyon had broken down. His face was buried in his arms, and he was a wreck of a man, sobbing like a hurt child.
evidence.paraphrase: Benyon collapses emotionally after failing to use the pistol.

evidence.quote: Even as the match gave out its flame, Mr Birdsey sprang.
evidence.paraphrase: Birdsey suddenly physically attacks Waterall to help Benyon escape.

evidence.quote: He isn't a crook. He's a fan. And we exiled fans have got to stick together.
evidence.paraphrase: Birdsey contrasts the legal view of Benyon as a criminal with his own view of him as a fellow enthusiast.
